Calculate the vertical drop from the release point ($60^\circ$) to the $30^\circ$ position:
$$h' = L(\cos 30^\circ - \cos 60^\circ) = 2.4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 0.5\right)$$
$$h' \approx 2.4(0.866025 - 0.5) = 2.4(0.366025) \approx 0.87846\text{ m}$$

Calculate the speed at this point by conservation of energy:
$$v = \sqrt{2gh'} = \sqrt{2(10)(0.87846)} = \sqrt{17.5692} \approx 4.19156\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 4.19\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

Explain why tension does no work:
$$\vec{T} \cdot d\vec{r} = T dr \cos 90^\circ = 0$$
The string tension is always directed radially towards $O$, perpendicular to the instantaneous tangential displacement of the particle along its circular arc. Therefore, the work done by tension is identically zero.

The speed at $30^\circ$ is $4.19\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

- Tension acts radially inwards while displacement is tangential:
$$W_T = 0$$
Because the angle between tension and motion is always $90^\circ$, tension transfers no energy.

hints: From $A$ to $B$, the vertical drop is $50 - 10 = 40\text{ m}$, so $v_B = \sqrt{2(10)(40)} = \sqrt{800} \approx 28.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
From $A$ to $C$, the vertical drop is $50 - 18 = 32\text{ m}$, so $v_C = \sqrt{2(10)(32)} = \sqrt{640} \approx 25.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Calculate the kinetic energy change between $B$ and $C$: $\frac{1}{2}m(v_C^2 - v_B^2) = 36(640 - 800) = -5760\text{ J}$.
Notice that this $-5760\text{ J}$ represents an identical gain in potential energy as the jumper rises $8\text{ m}$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the speed at dip $B$ ($40\text{ m}$ below starting point $A$):
$$v_B = \sqrt{2g(h_A - h_B)} = \sqrt{2(10)(50 - 10)} = \sqrt{800} \approx 28.284\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 28.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

Calculate the speed at take-off lip $C$ ($32\text{ m}$ below starting point $A$):
$$v_C = \sqrt{2g(h_A - h_C)} = \sqrt{2(10)(50 - 18)} = \sqrt{640} \approx 25.298\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 25.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

Determine the change in kinetic energy from $B$ to $C$:
$$\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}m(v_C^2 - v_B^2) = \frac{1}{2}(72)(640 - 800) = (36)(-160) = -5760\text{ J} \quad (-5.76\text{ kJ})$$
The kinetic energy decreases by $5760\text{ J}$ as the skier climbs from $10\text{ m}$ to $18\text{ m}$.

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Find speeds at dip and launch:
- Dropping $40\text{ m}$ to $B$:
$$v_B = \sqrt{800} \approx 28.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
- Dropping $32\text{ m}$ to $C$:
$$v_C = \sqrt{640} \approx 25.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

Calculate kinetic energy change on the ramp rise:
- Rising $8\text{ m}$ from $B$ to $C$ converts kinetic energy back to potential energy:
$$\Delta E_k = -mg\Delta h = -72(10)(8) = -5760\text{ J}$$
The jumper sacrifices $5.76\text{ kJ}$ of kinetic energy to gain altitude at the lip.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Capstone Practice 1: Ski jumper on smooth in-run ramp with dip, launch lip, and flight

hints: Because only gravity acts during flight, total mechanical energy is conserved all the way to ground level $D$ ($0\text{ m}$).
Landing speed depends solely on the total vertical drop of $50\text{ m}$: $v_D = \sqrt{2(10)(50)} = \sqrt{1000} \approx 31.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Total energy taking the bowl as zero is $E_{\text{total}} = mg(50) = 72(10)(50) = 36000\text{ J}$.
Kinetic energy at $C$ is $\frac{1}{2}(72)(640) = 23040\text{ J}$, so the percentage is $\frac{23040}{36000} \times 100\% = 64\%$.

walkthrough.text:
Apply energy conservation between initial release at $A$ ($h_A = 50\text{ m}$) and landing point $D$ ($h_D = 0\text{ m}$):
$$mg(50) = \frac{1}{2}mv_D^2 \implies v_D = \sqrt{2g(50)}$$
$$v_D = \sqrt{2(10)(50)} = \sqrt{1000} = 10\sqrt{10} \approx 31.6228\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 31.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

Calculate the total mechanical energy of the skier:
$$E_{\text{total}} = mgh_A = (72)(10)(50) = 36000\text{ J} \quad (36\text{ kJ})$$

Calculate the kinetic energy at launch point $C$ and determine the percentage:
$$E_{kC} = \frac{1}{2}mv_C^2 = \frac{1}{2}(72)(640) = 23040\text{ J}$$
$$\text{Percentage} = \frac{E_{kC}}{E_{\text{total}}} \times 100\% = \frac{23040}{36000} \times 100\% = 64\%$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Determine touch-down speed:
- Over the full $50\text{ m}$ descent, energy conservation gives:
$$v_D = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 50} = \sqrt{1000} \approx 31.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
The skier touches down at $31.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Analyze energy allocation at launch:
- Total mechanical energy: $36\text{ kJ}$
- Kinetic energy at lip: $23.04\text{ kJ}$
- Potential energy at lip: $12.96\text{ kJ}$:
$$\frac{23040}{36000} \times 100\% = 64\%$$
At the instant of take-off, $64\%$ of the skier's energy is kinetic and $36\%$ is potential.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Capstone Practice 2: Comparative descent on smooth versus rough inclined plane

hints: Vertical height descended is $h = 25\sin 18^\circ \approx 7.725\text{ m}$.
Initial kinetic energy is $\frac{1}{2}(8)(6^2) = 144\text{ J}$, and potential energy lost is $8(10)(7.7254) \approx 618.03\text{ J}$.
Total final kinetic energy on the smooth plane is $144 + 618.03 = 762.03\text{ J}$.
Solve for speed: $4v^2 = 762.03 \implies v = \sqrt{190.51} \approx 13.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the vertical height descended and potential energy lost:
$$h = d\sin 18^\circ = 25\sin 18^\circ \approx 7.7254\text{ m}$$
$$\Delta E_p = mgh = (8)(10)(25\sin 18^\circ) = 2000\sin 18^\circ \approx 618.034\text{ J}$$

Calculate initial kinetic energy and total mechanical energy:
$$E_{k0} = \frac{1}{2}mu^2 = \frac{1}{2}(8)(6^2) = 144\text{ J}$$
$$E_{kf} = E_{k0} + \Delta E_p = 144 + 618.034 = 762.034\text{ J}$$

Calculate the speed at the base of the smooth plane:
$$\frac{1}{2}(8)v_{\text{smooth}}^2 = 762.034 \implies 4v_{\text{smooth}}^2 = 762.034$$
$$v_{\text{smooth}}^2 = 190.5085 \implies v_{\text{smooth}} = \sqrt{190.5085} \approx 13.8025\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 13.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Compute energy balance on smooth slope:
- Starting kinetic energy: $144\text{ J}$
- Gravitational potential energy released: $618.03\text{ J}$:
$$E_{kf} = 144 + 618.03 = 762.03\text{ J}$$
No energy is lost on the smooth plane.

Solve for arrival velocity:
- Dividing by half the mass:
$$v_{\text{smooth}}^2 = \frac{762.03}{4} = 190.51 \implies v_{\text{smooth}} \approx 13.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
The block reaches $13.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

hints: Normal reaction is $R = mg\cos 18^\circ = 80\cos 18^\circ \approx 76.08\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the normal contact force and frictional force:
$$R = mg\cos 18^\circ = (8)(10)\cos 18^\circ = 80\cos 18^\circ \approx 76.0845\text{ N} \approx 76.1\text{ N}$$
$$F_r = \mu R = 0.15 \times 76.0845 \approx 11.4127\text{ N}$$

Calculate the work done against friction over the $25\text{ m}$ slide:
$$W_{\text{fric}} = F_r d = (11.4127)(25) = 285.317\text{ J} \approx 285\text{ J}$$

Apply the work-energy balance to determine the actual arrival speed:
$$E_{kf} = E_{k0} + \Delta E_p - W_{\text{fric}} = 762.034 - 285.317 = 476.717\text{ J}$$
$$\frac{1}{2}(8)v_{\text{rough}}^2 = 476.717 \implies 4v_{\text{rough}}^2 = 476.717$$
$$v_{\text{rough}}^2 = 119.179 \implies v_{\text{rough}} = \sqrt{119.179} \approx 10.9169\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 10.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
Friction dissipates $285\text{ J}$, reducing the speed by $2.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$ (from $13.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to $10.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$).
